nameStory: The shorthorn sculpin gets its name from the relatively short spines on its gill covers, which look like little horns compared to its cousin, the longhorn sculpin. "Sculpin" comes from an old word meaning "to carve," referring to their angular, carved-looking heads. Some old-timers also called it "bull-rout" because of its bulldog-like face and tendency to dart away when disturbed.
description: The shorthorn sculpin is a bottom-dwelling fish that looks like it was designed by someone who loved sharp angles and spines. This stocky, big-headed fish has a wide mouth, bulging eyes, and a body that tapers from a thick front to a narrow tail. They typically grow 6-12 inches long and spend their time hiding among rocks and seaweed on the ocean floor, perfectly camouflaged with their mottled brown and gray coloring.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Thick, angular head that's much wider than the narrow, tapering body - like a tadpole that's been carved from stone. The head feels bony and rigid to the touch.

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Large, fan-like pectoral fins that feel sturdy and are often held out like wings. The dorsal fin has both spiny and soft portions, with the spiny part having distinctly shorter spines than the longhorn sculpin.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Mottled brown, gray, and sometimes reddish patches that feel slightly rough to the touch. The pattern looks like camouflaged military fabric and changes slightly based on surroundings.

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Extremely wide mouth that opens downward - big enough that it could easily swallow a fish half its own size. The lips feel surprisingly soft compared to the bony head.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Usually 6-12 inches long, with the head making up about one-third of the total body length. Feels surprisingly heavy and solid for its size.

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found on rocky or sandy bottoms in cold ocean waters, often wedged between rocks or partially buried. Prefers areas with strong currents and cold temperatures.

habitat: Shorthorn sculpins live in the cold waters off New England's rocky coasts, particularly in deeper areas with strong currents. You'll find them on both rocky and sandy bottoms, from shallow tide pools down to depths of several hundred feet. They prefer areas where they can hide among rocks, kelp, or other bottom structures in the chilly waters from Maine down through Massachusetts.

seasonality.spring: Spawning season brings sculpins into shallower waters where they're more likely to be caught by anglers. Males may show slightly brighter coloration during breeding.
seasonality.summer: Most active feeding period when they're hunting crabs, worms, and small fish. Often found in deeper, cooler waters during the warmest months.
seasonality.fall: Feeding heavily before winter, making them more aggressive and easier to spot as they hunt in rocky areas and tide pools.
seasonality.winter: Less active in the coldest months but still present in deeper waters. Their cold-water adaptation means they remain more active than many other fish species.

funFact: Shorthorn sculpins are like the ultimate couch potatoes of the fish world - they can sit motionless for hours in the exact same spot, then suddenly explode into action to gulp down prey that's nearly as big as they are, thanks to their incredibly stretchy stomachs!
confusionNotes: Most often confused with the longhorn sculpin, but the shorthorn has much shorter spines on its gill covers - if the spines extend past the edge of the gill cover, it's probably a longhorn. Memory trick: "Short spines, shorthorn" - the spines shouldn't stick out noticeably beyond the head.
contextualKnowledge: This fish has an incredible variety of regional nicknames, including some colorful ones like "daddy sculpin" and "pig-fish" that reflect local fishing culture. Despite the intimidating spines and aggressive appearance, they're completely harmless to humans and are actually quite sluggish most of the time.
compareHints: Compared to the longhorn sculpin, the shorthorn has much shorter gill cover spines that don't extend past the gill edge. The grubby sculpin is much smaller and has a more streamlined body shape. Unlike both relatives, the shorthorn sculpin has the most robust, thick-set body shape and tends to be found in the coldest waters of the three species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relative the shorthorn sculpin, the longhorn has much more prominent gill spines and typically shows more distinct mottled patterning.
Grubbies are much smaller than their relatives the shorthorn and longhorn sculpins, rarely exceeding 6 inches compared to their cousins' 12+ inch lengths.
